new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand: primary stress falls on the first long (heavy) vowel of the word; if there is none, on the first syllable. Secondary stress is placed from the opposite (right) edge (code Ed). Weight is partly a matter of vowel quality (schwa syllables are light) and every word contains at least one non-light syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Goedemans code (Ed): secondary stress is located at, or footed from, the edge opposite the main stress. No first-hand statement seen.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in Goedemans; the entry is flagged '(quantity-sensitive: vowel quality, a word never consists of only light syllables)'. Breen 1976 (snippet) allows that stress may be phonemic.
new_statements.domain_note: Survey classification of the word-level pattern; no example words. Goedemans' own caveat (p.235) that entries deduced from limited material may be misplaced. The '(quantity-sensitive: vowel quality..)' note signals that the relevant weight is vowel quality (full vowel vs schwa), not only length; Jones 2000 (snippet) reports Breen 1992:10-11 as saying the syllable before a primary-stressed syllable has schwa, i.e. primary stress can be non-initial with pretonic reduction. Breen 1976 (snippet, first-hand) says only that 'length and/or stress may also be phonemic' and gives alternations like [núrmanand] vs [núrəmnándāgəl]; Black 1980:198 (held by the project) adds 'Stress is not transcribed for Kukatj, although Breen notes that it could conceivably be contrastive.'
new_statements.identity_note: Gugadj (Glottolog name) = Kukatj (AIATSIS G28, Breen's and Black's spelling), ISO ggd, Glottolog guga1239; a Paman language of the lower Flinders River near Normanton, not to be confused with Kukatja (kuka1246, Western Desert) or the Kokatha of South Australia. All sources examined describe this one variety (Breen's own corpus, one main speaker); Goedemans' 'Kukatj (T178)' is the same language.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's weight-sensitive reading (Goedemans 1998 from Breen 1992: first long vowel, else first syllable): the examples bear initial stress and Breen 1976 adds that schwa is never stressed and that stress interacts with schwa syncope. It does NOT state a rule, and its hedge that stress 'may also be phonemic' (echoed by Black 1980:198, 'Breen notes that it could conceivably be contrastive') is weaker than the predictable rule the catalog records from Breen 1992; treat as an earlier, less committed statement, not a contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Breen 1976 gives no placement rule. He says length and/or stress 'may also be phonemic' (i.e. possibly contrastive), that schwa never occurs in a stressed syllable, and that medial schwa presence depends on the stress pattern; his transcribed examples show stress on the first syllable ([núrmanand], [kámənand], [kámnánd]) with a second stress later in longer forms ([núrəmnándāgəl], [kámnánd]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the examples [núrəmnándāgəl] and [kámnánd] carry a second acute on a later syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the whole treatment is hedged ('may also be phonemic').
new_statements.identity_note: Breen 1976 calls the language 'Gugadj' (his 1992 spelling 'Kukatj'), spoken on the lower Flinders River, Gulf country, with Mayaguduna as western neighbour and Gog-Nar (Kok-Nar, kokn1236) as the contrasted Norman Pama language: this is guga1239. Thompson 1976 describes Kuuku-Ya'u of Lockhart River (with Umpila), a different Paman language on the east coast of Cape York.

readall_conflicts: No outright contradiction. Breen 1976 (the only primary work on Kukatj opened, search-snippet evidence) hedges that 'length and/or stress may also be phonemic' and gives no rule, while the catalog's weight-sensitive reading rests on Goedemans 1998's second-hand summary of Breen 1992 (first long vowel, else first syllable, secondary stress at the opposite edge, marginal quantity-sensitivity via vowel quality). Black 1980:198 relays the same 1976-era hedge ('Breen notes that it could conceivably be contrastive'). Breen 1976's examples are consistent with initial stress and with a later second stress, and his statement that schwa never bears stress fits the 1992 analysis (Jones 2000: the vowel before a primary-stressed syllable is schwa). The separate 'last lengthened vowel' rule visible in the same volume belongs to Thompson's Kuuku-Ya'u phonology (confirmed by Thompson 1988's identical wording), not to Kukatj. Breen 1992 itself (paywalled AJL) remains unopened, so the catalog's rule is still second-hand.
